claude.worst_flaw: The design names no replayable event or policy versioning, no staffed appeal beyond a single coordinator, and no explicit union agreement on data use or small-crew inference. holistic.reason: Well-designed with union co-design, verification, safety-hold parity, QA pause rules and a staggered test, but the 30-minute break is a modest reward, the process is heavy for one coordinator, and durable change depends on the app default and workflow fixes rather than the incentive.

codex.worst_flaw: The pilot leaves the timing of the checklist prompt and prefill unspecified across groups, so it could attribute gains from those workflow changes to the reward.

claude.worst_flaw: The audit trail is thin: there are no replayable event or policy versions, no independent shadow validation of the tally before payout, and no defined permissions or staffed timelines for appeals beyond a dispatch administrator correcting counts.

holistic.reason: Union co-design, independent verification, safety-first stop rules and a staggered lottery test make this approvable, though a 30-minute release reward is modest and durability rests on the app defaults and workflow fixes rather than the incentive itself.

claude.worst_flaw: Crew-level paid-time rewards can create peer pressure on individual technicians and the design does not say how crews are randomized and analysed when there are few crew pairs, how an expected effect size is powered, or whether early and late crews contaminate each other through shared dispatch boards. holistic.reason: Unusually well-designed (union co-design, independent verification, audit-based outcome measure, randomized stepped rollout, pause rules), but 30 minutes of paid time is a modest incentive and the rollout is heavy for one part-time coordinator, so the habit may fade unless the checklist becomes the default first step.

claude.worst_flaw: There is no appeal process and no versioned, replayable event or policy history. The lone review lead both audits and corrects the counts, and nothing independently validates the scoring, so disputed credits or exclusions cannot be checked transparently.

codex.worst_flaw: With only two rotations and no checks for differences in PR complexity or spillover between rotations, the pilot could mistake workload changes for a reward effect.

holistic.reason: Well-designed, skeptic-friendly program built on fixing workflow friction, private feedback, a shared team lunch, audit safeguards and a pre-committed decision rule, but it is complex to administer, the 45-minute cap looks tight, and with only two rotations the comparison is weak, so the staggered reward is only a minor motivator.

codex.worst_flaw: With one rotation per condition and no checks for differences in PR complexity or reviewer capacity, the pilot cannot reliably determine whether the lunch improved review turnaround.

claude.worst_flaw: The design has no replayable event or policy versioning and no independent shadow validation. holistic.reason: Well-designed with private feedback, fixed ownership, a quality audit and a clear handoff to automated routing, which suits sceptical engineers; the team lunch is a modest, collective reward that may go unnoticed, and the six-week pilot with two small rotations gives only directional evidence on whether the improvement lasts.

claude.worst_flaw: The squad lunch is posted publicly in the engineering channel and depends on the whole squad's on-time share, which creates peer pressure for rushed reviews, yet the only check on review depth is a 10-PR weekly sample with no measure of displacement into other engineering work or of PR size and case mix.

codex.worst_flaw: The primary metric is unsuitable for a launch decision because a substantive, on-time change request or blocking question can go uncounted if the author never responds, biasing the measured rate in favor of approvals.

holistic.reason: It fixes routing and protected time first, uses a verified outcome metric with an audit sample, keeps individual data private, and ends with a retire-the-reward decision, which suits sceptical engineers. codex.worst_flaw: The pilot lacks an immediate stop rule when kiosk use is found to interrupt patient care.

holistic.reason: Rewarding audited compliance rather than kiosk logging, with staggered rollout, sample safeguards, privacy limits and pause rules, is sound and approvable, but a monthly team meal tied to a five-point gain is a modest, delayed incentive that nurses may barely notice, and gains may fade once the meals stop.

codex.worst_flaw: The pilot has a launch-blocking measurement gap because it can repeat the reward based on audited compliance without knowing whether nurses log more eligible hand-hygiene moments at the kiosk.

holistic.reason: Rigorous, audit-anchored team reward with staggered randomisation, gaming safeguards and nurse-driven kiosk fixes is approvable, but a one-off shared meal for two months will be weakly salient and unlikely to sustain behaviour once rewards stop, with only the kiosk defaults and feedback carrying over.

claude.worst_flaw: The kiosk logs that the scenario is about play no part in the reward or the decision. codex.worst_flaw: The pilot uses audited hand hygiene to decide whether to keep the kiosk, even though its comparison tests the meal incentive and raw submission counts cannot show what share of eligible moments nurses logged.

holistic.reason: Well-designed with sound measurement, protected audit, and staff-friendly kiosk fixes, but a shared ward meal is a weak, delayed incentive, the logging itself isn't rewarded, and without ongoing reinforcement the effect likely fades after rewards stop.

codex.worst_flaw: The reward decision hinges on a two-point difference in a two-week team comparison without checking whether the number of teams and tickets can distinguish that effect from ordinary variation.

holistic.reason: Well-guarded design with QA checks, team-level rewards and a staggered comparison, but it is complex to run for a 60-person org, the 15-point target is demanding, and the gains may fade once rewards and defaults end.

codex.worst_flaw: The primary decision metric is a launch blocker because teams can improve their seven-day resolution rate by leaving difficult tickets open, and the pilot measures neither backlog nor time to resolution.

claude.worst_flaw: The decision test depends on a few paired teams over only two weeks, with no sample-size, uncertainty or spillover handling, and the scoring has no replayable event or policy versions or shadow validation.

holistic.reason: Well-designed with agent co-design, private feedback, QA sampling, stepped-wedge evaluation and CSAT guardrails, but the rule is complex to explain, the reward (one paid hour, team-level) is modest and diffuse, and 7-day credit delay plus heavy exclusions/verification may blunt salience and add admin burden.

codex.worst_flaw: The pilot sets a two-percentage-point success threshold without checking whether two weeks of data from the available teams can distinguish that gain from normal variation in case mix and repeat contacts.

claude.worst_flaw: The design never settles how the existing CSAT bonus interacts with the article goal, and it has no versioned event log, independent shadow validation or staffed appeal beyond a QA channel, so a disputed eligibility call ("an article would have helped") is subjective and hard to audit.

holistic.reason: Well-designed with verification, randomized rollout, QA sampling and a durable-resolution outcome measure, but it is complex for a 60-person org (two-week listening phase, rolling baselines, provisional credit, reopen reversals) and the reward is only one hour of development time, so motivation and persistence after it ends are modest.
